passage: In the open-plan office in Prague, Vera watched Emil present the project update to the director and felt her face burn. He's trying to take the credit, she thought. He always does. She was already drafting a sharp message in her head. Then she stopped, coffee halfway to her lips, and asked herself the question her old mentor used to ask: is any of this in me? The answer came fast and uncomfortable. She wanted the director to notice her. She had wanted to present it herself. Emil had simply been asked. The heat drained out of her. She didn't send the message. Instead she asked her manager for a chance to present the next phase.

qa.q: Where did this happen?
qa.a: In the open-plan office in Prague.

qa.q: What did Vera feel as Emil presented?
qa.a: Her face burned; she felt angry and certain he was stealing credit, until she saw her own wish to be noticed.

qa.q: What did Vera's question change?
qa.a: Asking "is any of this in me?" revealed her own wish for credit, took the heat out, and led her to ask for what she actually needed, a chance to present.

qa.q: What would have changed for Emil if Vera had sent the sharp message?
qa.a: He would have been accused of something he hadn't done, since he had simply been asked, and their working relationship would suffer.

grounding: An adult certain that a colleague is grabbing credit pauses to see the same wish in herself, which cools her and shows what she needs.

qa.a: "What part of this is mine?"

qa.a: Her face lit up; she seemed happy and relieved to have a partner rather than a rival.

grounding: An adult certain about a colleague's bad motive asks what part is her own, and finds her own competitiveness and need.

qa.a: Harsha feels guilty about skipping revision, and blaming the exam feels better tonight than facing that.

qa.q: What did Shankar do that helped?
qa.a: Asked "everyone who?", reminded Harsha of the engineering goal without lecturing, and agreed to a study call at 7.

qa.q: How might Shankar be feeling during the chat?
qa.a: Concerned but careful not to preach, wanting to help a friend face it.

grounding: A teenager who skipped study decides the exam is rigged and marks don't matter, easing shame now while raising the cost later.

passage: On the bus back from the district town, Yogesh stared out at the sugarcane fields. The board maths exam had been a disaster, and he hadn't studied much; he had spent his evenings at the pond with friends. "The paper was out of syllabus," he told Akash. "Totally unfair. And marks don't matter anyway. I'll just work on the farm." Akash frowned. "You told me you wanted to be a vet." Yogesh shrugged, but his throat felt tight. It was easier to hate the paper than to remember the pond. At home his mother asked how it went. He opened his mouth to say "unfair", then said instead, "I didn't prepare, Aai." She sat down beside him. "Then let's see what we can do for the supplementary."

qa.q: Where had Yogesh spent his evenings?
qa.a: At the pond with friends.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh call the paper unfair?
qa.a: He felt ashamed that he hadn't prepared, and blaming the paper eased the shame for now.

qa.q: What changed when he spoke to his mother?
qa.a: He admitted he hadn't prepared, and she responded by planning for the supplementary, turning the story into action.

qa.q: How does Akash see Yogesh's claim that marks don't matter?
qa.a: Akash is doubtful, reminding him he wanted to be a vet, and perhaps worried for him.

grounding: A teenager who didn't prepare calls the exam unfair and says marks don't matter, then admits the truth to his mother.

passage: The email came while Trisha was on the Kolkata metro: "We regret to inform you..." The scholarship for the summer programme in Singapore had gone to someone else. By the time she met Leela at the coffee house, she had a whole speech ready. "Honestly, I never really wanted it. The programme's overrated. Two months of lectures in that heat? No thanks." Leela listened, then said, "You rewrote your essay four times." Trisha shrugged. "Waste of time." But her fingers kept turning the cup. Leela said gently, "You're allowed to be gutted. And maybe you could ask them for feedback, for next year." Trisha looked away. "Maybe," she said. "Maybe I did want it."

qa.q: How many times did Trisha rewrite her essay?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: Why does Trisha say she never wanted the scholarship?
qa.a: She is deeply disappointed, and telling herself the programme was overrated eases the sting.

qa.q: What does Leela suggest?
qa.a: That it's okay to be gutted, and that asking for feedback for next year would let the attempt teach something.

qa.q: How does Leela see Trisha's speech?
qa.a: She sees through it, remembering the four rewrites, and responds kindly rather than arguing.

grounding: A student rejected for a scholarship says she never wanted it and the programme is overrated, hiding both disappointment and lessons.

passage:
"Did you hear back about the research fellowship?"
"Didn't get it."
"Oh, Zainab. I'm sorry."
"It's fine, Urmila. I didn't really want it. Too much paperwork. And their research is so boring."
"You told me their research was the reason you applied."
"I've changed my mind."
"Since yesterday?"
Zainab looked at her tea. "It's easier to think it was bad."
"Easier than what?"
"Than thinking I wasn't good enough."
"Or that your proposal needed work. Those aren't the same thing."
"...They're not, are they."
"Ask them for comments. Then decide if it's boring."

qa.q: What reason did Zainab first give for applying?
qa.a: Their research.

qa.q: Why does Zainab now say the research is boring?
qa.a: Zainab is hurt by the rejection, and calling the fellowship bad is easier than feeling not good enough.

qa.q: What does Urmila suggest?
qa.a: Asking the fellowship for comments before deciding it's boring, and separating "not good enough" from "the proposal needed work".

qa.q: How might Urmila feel hearing Zainab's excuses?
qa.a: Sympathetic but gently persistent, wanting her friend not to lose the lesson.

grounding: A student rejected for a fellowship calls it boring and unwanted to ease disappointment, until a friend questions it.

passage: Two years ago I applied for the state merit scholarship and didn't get it. Within an hour I had decided I never wanted it anyway. I told my friend Yogesh the programme was for "bookworms", that the stipend was tiny, that I would have hated the rules. I said it so often I almost believed it. Yogesh just said, "Okay, Santosh," in a way that annoyed me. Months later, helping a junior apply, I read the selection criteria properly for the first time. Community work: I had none. Interview practice: I had skipped it. That hurt more than the rejection. The sour story had kept me from learning anything. This year I applied again, with both. I got an interview.

qa.q: What did Santosh first call the programme?
qa.a: Something for "bookworms".

qa.q: What made Santosh feel more hurt than the rejection itself?
qa.a: Realising, while helping a junior, that the sour story had hidden clear gaps in community work and interview practice and kept Santosh from learning.

qa.q: What did Santosh do differently the second time?
qa.a: Built up community work and practised interviews before applying again, and got an interview.

qa.q: How might Yogesh have felt hearing Santosh's excuses?
qa.a: Probably sceptical but patient, saying "Okay, Santosh" rather than arguing.

grounding: A student rejected for a scholarship tells a sour-grapes story that eases disappointment but hides what could be learned.

passage:
"So the report slipped because the data came late."
"Okay," said Gurpreet.
"And also the client changed the format. And, honestly, the brief was unclear from the start."
"This morning you said the data was fine."
"Well, it was fine, but late-ish. And then there was the server issue."
"The server issue was last month, Ira."
"It had knock-on effects."
Gurpreet noticed Ira's reasons growing longer and neater, like a lawyer's. She didn't push. She just asked, "Is something about this project making you uneasy?"
Ira paused. The polish dropped out of her voice. "I'm not sure I know how to do the analysis. I didn't want to say."
"Okay. Let's look at it together."

qa.q: When was the server issue?
qa.a: Last month.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet notice, and what did she feel?
qa.a: She noticed Ira's reasons growing longer, neater and changing, and felt curious and gently concerned that something uncomfortable lay underneath.

qa.q: What made Gurpreet's question effective?
qa.a: Instead of arguing with each reason, she asked whether something about the project made Ira uneasy, which let the real worry come out.

qa.q: What was Ira actually feeling?
qa.a: Worried and embarrassed about not knowing how to do the analysis, hidden behind tidy reasons.

grounding: A colleague hears a peer's changing, polished excuses and gently asks what feels uncomfortable underneath.

passage: Last quarter my colleague Kamal promised to send the vendor list by Friday. On Monday I asked, and got a ten-minute explanation: the vendors had changed prices, the finance team was slow, the template was outdated. By Wednesday the reasons had changed: now it was a family function and a laptop crash. Each story was tidy and sensible. That was what bothered me. When I'm honestly late, my excuse is one short, embarrassed sentence. So I stopped arguing with the reasons. I said, "Kamal, it sounds like this task has been uncomfortable." He laughed, then didn't. "I called two vendors and they were rude. I've been avoiding it." I'm Omkar, by the way, and we made the calls together. It took forty minutes.

qa.q: How long did the vendor calls take together?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Kamal's explanations make Omkar uneasy?
qa.a: They were tidy, sensible and kept changing, which made Omkar uneasy and suspicious that something else was going on.

qa.q: What did Omkar do instead of disputing the reasons?
qa.a: Said the task seemed uncomfortable, which let Kamal admit avoiding rude vendors, and then they made the calls together.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling underneath the excuses?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable and anxious after two rude vendor calls, and was avoiding the task.

grounding: A colleague notices a peer's reasons keep changing and are too tidy, and gently names the discomfort underneath.

passage: Supervisor's note, Friday. Joseph promised the training module by the 10th. When I asked today, he explained for nearly fifteen minutes: the software update, then Raghav's late slides, then a policy change, then a clash with another deadline. Raghav, sitting nearby, looked puzzled; his slides had gone in on the 3rd. What struck me was how smooth it all was, and how often it shifted. I didn't argue. I asked, "What's the hardest part of this module for you?" Joseph was silent, then said he had never taught adults before and was dreading recording himself. We have booked a practice session with our trainer for Monday.

qa.q: When did Raghav's slides go in?
qa.a: On the 3rd.

qa.q: What did the supervisor notice and feel while Joseph explained?
qa.a: The supervisor was struck by how smooth and shifting the reasons were and felt a quiet suspicion that something uncomfortable lay underneath, but stayed calm.

qa.q: What question helped, and what came of it?
qa.a: "What's the hardest part of this module for you?" It revealed Joseph's dread of recording himself, and a practice session was booked.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel hearing his slides blamed?
qa.a: Puzzled and perhaps a bit annoyed, since his slides had gone in on the 3rd.

grounding: A supervisor notices a colleague's excuses are smooth and shifting, and a gentle question uncovers the real discomfort.
